Subject: Performance SLO follow-up: context window / token limits and latency impact (FinCo)

John / Samantha — thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap and proposed next steps so we can align on performance SLOs and technical validation.

Call highlights (as we captured):
- Primary SLO: p95 latency target of 300ms for short responses (<=256 output tokens) under peak workload.
- Streaming is required for the user-facing experience (partial outputs must be delivered within ~150–200ms of the first token).
- Peak throughput: ~100–150 requests/sec (spread across multiple endpoints).
- Target concurrency (per model endpoint): 40–80 concurrent sessions during peak trading hours.
- Context window needs: up to 25k input tokens (historical context + prompts); outputs expected up to 2k tokens for long-form explanations, though most responses are short.

Open questions we agreed to validate:
1) How latency scales with context window size and output token length (non-streaming vs streaming).
2) Acceptable tail latency for long outputs (we discussed softer SLOs for >512 tokens).
3) Whether prefix/KV caching can be used for repeated context to reduce p95.
4) Exact payloads and tokenization characteristics (sample records from FinCo to benchmark).

Next steps (proposed):
- I will share a short benchmark pack and sample payloads (attached) with numbers from comparable workloads.
- Schedule a 60-min technical deep-dive with our inference engineers (Rishi) to run a focused benchmark with your sample payloads. Proposed slots: Wed 14 Oct 10:00–11:00 PT or Thu 15 Oct 09:00–10:00 PT.
- If possible, please share a representative sample of 10–20 queries (anonymized) that include: average input size, extremes (largest context), and expected output length.

Attachments: finco_slo_table.xlsx (your notes template), sample_payloads.json (example payloads), SLO_latency_benchmarks_Q42026.pdf (Redwood internal summary).

Thanks — I’ll wait for the sample payloads and a preferred slot for the deep-dive.

John — great questions. Below are concrete answers and the context behind the numbers. I’ve attached our benchmark pack and sample payloads so your team can sanity-check tokenization and sizes before the deep-dive.

Short summary (high-level):
- Baseline used for numbers: rwd-large variant on Dedicated instance type D-8 (8 A100-class GPUs), concurrency maintained at 20 per model replica, typical batch window ~5–8ms.
- Small outputs (<=256 tokens): p95 ~200–260ms with 4k context; p95 grows to ~300–360ms with 25k context (mostly due to self-attention and KV cache handling).
- Streaming: reduces perceived latency for users — first byte delivered typically 60–120ms faster than non-streaming start-of-response. End-to-end p95 for full 256-token outputs is similar, but UX is much better because users see partial results earlier.
- Long outputs (1k–2k tokens): p95 for full completion will be higher (1.2s–2.5s depending on context and concurrency). We typically recommend separate SLOs for long-form generation (e.g., p95 < 2.5s) and stricter ones for short responses.

Notes & levers: 
- Context window impact: the self-attention compute scales roughly O(n^2) with sequence length for some kernels — larger contexts noticeably increase per-token latency for the first few tokens and for KV cache population. For many finance workloads where context is mostly lookup/history, prefix/KV caching can reduce p95 by 30–60% for repeated contexts.
- Tokenization: whitespace-heavy financial data can tokenize densely; the same 1,000 characters may produce different token counts depending on structure. That’s why we ask for sample payloads.
- Batching and concurrency: throughput gains from batching come with trade-offs for tail latency. Continuous/bounded batching in our runtime limits batch-wait to a few ms to protect p95. If you need strict 300ms p95 at 150 rps, Dedicated with pinned capacity is the safest path.
- Streaming vs non-streaming: streaming gives immediate partial outputs and reduces user-perceived latency. It requires client support for chunked responses and our SDKs/websocket endpoints handle reassembly and ordering.
- Fallbacks & model variants: we can automatically route shorter/latency-sensitive requests to lower-context model variants (8k or 4k) while routing long-context requests to large-context variants; this lets you keep tight SLOs on core product flows.

Attached are the benchmark numbers broken down by: context size (4k / 8k / 16k / 25k), output length (32 / 128 / 256 / 1024 / 2048 tokens), concurrency (10 / 20 / 40), and streaming vs non-streaming. See SLO_latency_benchmarks_Q42026.pdf.

Recommended next steps (concrete):
1) Please share the anonymized 10–20 representative payloads (or confirm that the sample_payloads.json we attached is close).
2) Confirm a 60-min deep-dive with your infra team — Rishi will run the benchmark and we’ll capture p50/p95/p99 across your payloads. Proposed times: Wed 14 Oct, 10:00–11:00 PT (preferred).
3) If you want, we can provision a short Dedicated trial (48–72 hrs) to run your live workload; we’ll need a signed trial addendum (we can send a one-click DocuSign).

I’ll add the benchmark pack to the shared Drive link included below.
